CXC-CARTHING-INPUTS.title: Encoder + Switches Are Tier-1 Input HAL

CXC-BRINGUP-INTENT.title: Systematize Bring-Up, From Flash Loops to a Descriptor Surface

properties.problem: every new board is a fresh ad-hoc flash loop with the hard-won facts scattered across a platformio.ini, commit messages, and a person's memory. The real cost is concrete and recent: **this cycle's CYD shared-SPI-DMA-channel hunt** (a staged hardware bisection to find that an SD-bus `spi_bus_free()` teardown froze the panel while it kept ACKing writes) and **the CH32V203 wchisp/BOOT0 dance** (a manual ISP strap that is easy to get wrong and has no software entry) both cost real hours that a descriptor + a surface would have front-loaded.
properties.definition: a bring-up discipline where each board has ONE machine-readable descriptor (`docs/board-bringup/<board>.descriptor.yaml`) carrying identity, connect, flash, config-source, requires, verify, and quirks — and a control surface that consumes it to connect/flash/verify/record a node. Same discipline as [CXC-HAL]: define-once descriptor over per-platform drivers, generalized from *binding a peripheral* to *standing up a whole board*.
properties.grounded: FOUR real boards brought up this cycle prove the schema is not hypothetical — the constrained SPI-display floor (CYD), the framebuffer-tier round panel (Qualia S3), the reactive/actuator RISC-V tier (ESP32-C3 devkit + lego_dots + rack_triple_gauge), and the first non-ESP32/non-esptool part (CH32V203, wchisp). Four divergent ad-hoc descriptor shapes reconciled into one.
properties.payoff: a new board = author a descriptor + (if novel) register its flash tool, not reinvent a flash loop; a new physical unit = point the surface at it and press one gated button.

CXC-BRINGUP-DESCRIPTOR.title: The Per-Board Descriptor Is the Single Source; the Recipe Is a Generated View

properties.define-once: the descriptor is the SINGLE SOURCE. The markdown recipe (`docs/board-bringup/<board>.md`) demotes to a **generated human view**; the app/surface consumes the descriptor, not the prose — exactly the [CXC-HAL-PLATFORM] "define-once descriptor" move applied to a board. Divergence between recipe and descriptor becomes impossible because the recipe is rendered FROM the descriptor.
properties.requires: = reproducible-from-the-bus: board-specific images/packages/blobs a bring-up needs are named as `requires:` references (David's directive — any image/package a board needs lives in `bus_storage` and is fetched at bring-up, reproducible from the bus). Grounded: the CYD/Qualia scene config (`bus://assets/displays/<device_id>.compose.yaml`, the [CXC-R-BOOT] fungible-fetch) and the animation assets (`bus://assets/animations/dradis/*`, CI16 sprite frames baked offline). Where an artifact does not exist yet (a bus-hosted factory firmware image, a board package-set), it is recorded as a `null` placeholder WITH a comment naming where it WOULD live (`bus://assets/firmware/<board>/<ver>.bin`) — the gap is explicit, not silent. Non-bus prerequisites are honestly typed (the C3's gitignored `src/wifi_config.h` secret, the `mqtt://192.0.2.75:1883` transport) rather than faked as bus assets.

CXC-BRINGUP-DISPATCH.title: Flash-Tool + Entry Dispatch Off the Descriptor

CXC-BRINGUP-SURFACE.title: Generalize [minnow-bringup] — One Control Surface Stands Up Any Node

CXC-HALD-INTENT.title: Physical I/O as a Code-Free Bus-Peer Declaration

properties.definition: a peripheral is declared, not coded. One `peripheral:` entry states WHICH physical port/address, WHICH interface kind + params, WHICH driver decodes it, and WHICH semantic namespace(s) it publishes/subscribes/commands. The runtime on the owning peer reads the declaration and instantiates the driver. No per-sensor code in the scene — the look-and-feel of `.compose.yaml` widgets, applied to silicon.

CXC-HALD-KINDS.title: The Nine Interface Kinds (the Closed Set) + the `adaptor` Family

properties.definition: a peripheral's `interface` is EXACTLY ONE kind. This closed set covers 100% of the Grove/Qwiic cross-section (grove-peripheral-cross-section.md §10); each carries a small fixed parameter set:
change: decision: INTERFACE KIND (not device) is the top-level axis; transports are separate.

reasoning: "The device space is huge (400+ SKUs) but the interface space is tiny and closed (nine kinds). One `i2c{addr,driver}` line covers dozens of chips. Keying on device would produce 400 schemas and re-invent a driver library. Transports were tempting to add as a tenth kind, but `can_controller` shows CAN is a peer-to-peer FABRIC, not a peripheral — modeling it as a kind would have conflated 'a thing that publishes temperature' with 'the wire the bus rides on'."

CXC-HALD-TOPOLOGY.title: Bus-Shared vs Point-to-Point — and Hierarchical Addressing

properties.definition: the primary axis. `i2c`/`onewire`/`spi` are **bus-shared** — many devices per bus, each needing a SELECTOR (I2C `addr`, 1-Wire `rom`, SPI `cs`). `analog`/`digital_in`/`pwm_out`/`uart`/`single_wire`/`ws281x` are **point-to-point**. BUT real builds interpose **addressing layers**, so a selector/pin is a PATH, not a flat value:
properties.selector-required: a bus-shared kind without its selector is rejected ([CXC-HALD-VALIDATE]); a collision is a duplicate selector on the SAME segment (post-mux), not merely the same address.
change: decision: addressing is HIERARCHICAL (a path), not flat.

reasoning: "Two independent sources forced this. The Grove catalog has the TCA9548A (same-address coexistence) and the CD74HC4067 analog mux; and on real hardware, MCP23017 expanders appear on TWO of the four boards ([PCB-BTNMATRIX] runs 2×, [PCB-GAUGE3] runs 1×). A flat `addr`/`pin` model can't express any of it, and the v1 collision rule was simply wrong. Hierarchical addressing is the minimal correct model and it makes expanders/muxes first-class rather than special-cased."

properties.definition: a whole class of parts are not sensors/actuators but **port-providers** — they consume one bus/pin and RE-EXPOSE N virtual pins/channels that other peripherals address through. The declaration models them as a peripheral with a `provides:` clause:
properties.grounded: `[PCB-BTNMATRIX]` is the canonical case — 2× MCP23017 (0x20 buttons, 0x21 LEDs) turn one I2C bus into 32 addressable pins for 16 buttons + 16 LEDs. `[PCB-GAUGE3]` uses an MCP23017 (0x20) to fan out to 3 H-bridges. The port-provider is declared once; the leaf peripherals address through it.
properties.runtime: the port-provider's driver owns the expansion (register writes to set/read MCP pins, channel-select on the mux); a peripheral addressed `pin: mcp0.gpa3` is transparently routed by the runtime. Chainable providers compose (`sr0.bit5`, `mux0.ch2 → 0x44`).

CXC-HALD-DRIVER.title: `driver` — the Join Key to the Decode Registry (and to Built Drivers)

properties.definition: for `i2c`/`uart`/`onewire`/`single_wire`/`spi`/`ws281x`/port-providers, the raw stream is meaningless without a per-chip/per-protocol DECODER. `driver` names it — `bme280`, `vl53l0x`, `ssd1306`, `nmea`, `pn532`, `ds18b20`, `mcp23017`, `x27168`, `mcp2515`. It is the JOIN KEY to a decoder registry (register maps / protocol framers, authored per chip, delivered as ARTIFACTS — [CXC-HALD-DRIVER-DIST]) AND to EXISTING ComposeIO drivers: `pn532`→`composeio.peripherals.nfc`; `ws281x`→WLED family; `buzzer`/`mp3`/`dac`→audio. A driver self-describes (interface kind + params, provides?, published/subscribed namespaces, config schema, assurance class) so the Composer palette can generate from it.

CXC-HALD-ROLE.title: Sensor Publishes · Actuator Subscribes · Transactional Commands

properties.definition: THREE role shapes (v3 adds the third, from the R503):
properties.dual-role: a peripheral may combine roles (PN532 read/write; a Grove LCD-RGB = `display/text` + `led/color`; a slide-pot = `input/slider` sensor + on-board LED actuator) — one entry, a namespace map tagged by role.

CXC-HALD-NAMESPACE.title: Namespaces by Physical Quantity, Not by Part (the Define-Once Enabler)

properties.definition: the semantic namespace names a PHYSICAL QUANTITY, never a chip. `env/temperature` is published identically by a BME280, SHT31, DS18B20, thermistor, or a DS3231 die sensor — so a widget/rule/Intelligence/peer binds the quantity and is indifferent to the silicon; swap the sensor, the scene is unchanged. Illustrative vocabulary (grouped): `env/{temperature,humidity,pressure,altitude}`, `air/{co2,tvoc,voc_index,pm/2_5,gas/*}`, `light/{lux,uv_index,color}`, `motion/{accel,gyro,mag}/{x,y,z}`, `motion/{heading,steps,vibration}`, `distance/mm`, `presence/{detected,target/{n}/{x,y,speed}}`, `geo/position/{lat,lon,alt}`, `touch/key/{n}`, `rotation/angle`, `time/rtc`, `fingerprint/{match,enroll/status}`; actuators: `relay/{n}/state`, `servo/angle`, **`gauge/value`**, **`motor/{speed,direction,position}`**, `buzzer/{state,tone}`, `led/{state,brightness,color}`, `display/{text}`, `haptic/effect`. Diagnostics/health (any peripheral, a first-class convention not a per-part afterthought): `.../fault`, `.../open`, `.../short`, `.../health` — e.g. a PCA995x LED driver publishes `led/{n}/fault`, making an actuator DUAL-ROLE (it drives AND self-reports).

CXC-HALD-COMPOUND.title: Compound Peripherals — Groups, Actuator Pin-Groups, Banks

properties.definition: many real peripherals are ONE logical/semantic object built from MANY physical pins/elements. Three shapes, all declared as a single grouped peripheral (not N scattered atomics):
properties.grounded: three of the four boards are compound — `[PCB-BTNMATRIX]` (matrix), `[PCB-GAUGE3]` (3× actuator pin-groups + a 3-gauge cluster), `[PCB-LEGODOTS]` (12× bank). The atomic-only v1/v2 schema would have scattered each into dozens of unrelated lines.

properties.definition: a top-level `peripherals:` list (board profile or `.compose.yaml` deployment section). Each entry: `{ id, on?, role, interface:{<kind>:{params}}, driver, provides?, namespace|namespaces, config?, assurance? }`. `on:` names the owning PEER (an MCU id or `host`) — so one schema covers an MCU-attached Grove sensor and a host-side adaptor. Worked example — a real mixed board that exercises hierarchical addressing, a compound actuator, and config:
properties.runtime: each peer filters `peripherals` for its own `on:`, instantiates port-providers first, then the peripherals addressed through them, wiring sensors→publish / actuators→subscribe / transactional→cmd+status+result. MCU firmware and host service use the same declaration; only the owned subset differs.
change: decision: ONE unified `peripherals:` list (role + `on:` + `provides:` tags), port-providers declared inline.

reasoning: "Sensor/actuator/transactional/adaptor and MCU/host differ only in fields, not schema. A unified list keeps one mental model, lets a dual-role part be one entry, and — the surfacing answer to 'what does ComposeUX need for these' — makes the built WLED/audio/NFC and a future Grove sensor and a real board's expander all declare the same way."

CXC-HALD-CONFIG.title: Device Configuration & Calibration (Persistent, Distinct from Live Namespaces)

properties.definition: nearly every non-trivial peripheral needs PERSISTENT configuration/calibration distinct from its live namespaces — LD2410 per-gate sensitivity, LD2420 range/timeout, INA219 shunt resistance, the 0–25V divider's `calibrate_linear` points, servo/gauge trim, a stepper's `sweep_deg`/home, TCA8418 debounce. It is set-once/tuned-in-situ, PERSISTED, and applied by the driver at init. Declared in a peripheral's `config:` block; the driver's self-description carries the config schema.

CXC-HALD-VALIDATE.title: Collision & Allocation Validation (Fail at Parse, Not on the Bench)

properties.definition: the validator MUST catch, before deploy: (1) **selector collisions on a segment** — a duplicate I2C `addr` on the SAME bus/mux-channel (a mux RESOLVES it — same addr on different channels is fine); duplicate 1-Wire `rom` / SPI `cs`. (2) **pin conflicts** — two point-to-point peripherals on the same resolved pin (including expander sub-pins: two things on `io.gpa0`). (3) **provider over-allocation** — more sub-pins/channels claimed than a provider `provides:`. (4) **selector-required / driver-unknown** — rejected with a "did you mean" from the registry. (5) **shared-provider agreement** — channels on a single-prescaler provider (PCA9685) must share a compatible PWM frequency; a 50 Hz servo channel and a 1 kHz LED channel on the SAME PCA9685 is rejected (chain a second PCA9685 at another address). This is the whole payoff of declaring-before-building: the wiring mistake is caught at parse time, not with a multimeter.

CXC-HALD-RULES.title: Local Reaction Rules at the Leaf

properties.definition: a peripheral reacts to another (or to imported ComposeBus intent) via a DECLARATIVE rule that runs AT THE LEAF on the MCU's INTERNAL bus, using the EXISTING logic layer ([SPEC:CXC-BIND] behaviors, the [SPEC:CXC-FLAUTH] headless node, the [plt.cux:SPEC:CXC-DSL] expression DSL) — NOT a new HAL rule engine. `rules:` declares `when <condition over internal namespaces> → set <internal namespace(s)>`. Local, fast, and it SURVIVES loss of the ComposeBus link (autonomy at the leaf).
change: decision: reuse the existing headless-logic layer scoped to the internal bus, not a HAL-specific engine.

reasoning: "The platform already has a declarative no-code logic surface that runs on ANY ComposeIOBus; the MCU's internal bus IS one. A HAL-specific engine would fork a solved problem. The HAL's job is only to STATE that rules run at the leaf and make the internal bus a first-class place to run them."

CXC-HALD-BRIDGE.title: The Internal Bus ↔ ComposeBus Membrane — Pluggable Transport, Authority-Gated

properties.definition: a device has TWO buses; the HAL models the membrane. The MCU is a ComposeApp with an INTERNAL bus (local scope) and a COMPOSEBUS connection (shared/global). The membrane is config-driven, reusing ComposeApp export/import + `Scope` ([plt.cio:SPEC:DP-CIO-5]):
change: decision: model the two buses + a PLUGGABLE transport + authority-gating explicitly, reusing ComposeApp's bridge.

reasoning: "The acid test showed a device always has two buses; the real boards showed the membrane rides different fabrics (MQTT, CAN, UART-relay) — CAN is a peer-to-peer transport, not a peripheral, so it belongs here. And a fingerprint/relay/launch semantic must be gate-able. Default-local + explicit-export + authority-gated-command is the safe direction."

CXC-HALD-DRIVER-DIST.title: The Driver as a Signed, Tiered, Fetchable BusStorage Artifact

properties.definition: a `driver` reaches the peer that needs it as a SIGNED artifact from BusStorage (`bus://drivers/<id>@<ver>`, content-addressed, verified against the bus Authority/CA BEFORE load). "Driver" is not one thing — it is three artifact TIERS, and the tier determines how (and whether) it loads at runtime:
change: decision: driver = a signed BusStorage artifact in three tiers, data-descriptor-first, VM for the complex, OTA for the floor.

reasoning: "The trap is treating every driver as a native-code plugin — uniformly hard AND a supply-chain hole. Splitting by artifact tier makes the common case (register-map sensors) pure signed DATA interpreted by a generic engine (no code loading), quarantines the hard VM path to the stateful minority, and honestly bottoms out at OTA on the floor. The R503 pins the VM's requirements (framing, checksum, timers, KB buffers, resume); the real boards anchor the tiers to actual silicon."

CXC-HALD-MINE.title: The Open-Source Ecosystem as the Registry's Seed — Mine, Don't Run

properties.definition: the Home Assistant + ESPHome ecosystems are the largest open-source device-support corpus in existence (thousands of integrations, hundreds of ESPHome components). The registry ([CXC-HALD-DRIVER]) is SEEDED by MINING them — reading the open source to AUTHOR HAL drivers — and ComposeIO runs NO HA/ESPHome plugin code to do it. Two flavors, by how self-contained the source is:
properties.why: this turns the world's biggest device library into ComposeIO's driver registry with no runtime dependency on HA and no per-chip authoring slog — the single largest accelerant for coverage and the OSS-adoption on-ramp.

CXC-HALD-ASSURANCE.title: The Assurance Class — Don't Imply Guarantees You Can't Back

properties.definition: a peripheral declares an `assurance` class so the HAL never over-promises: `experiential` (a prop/effect — a consumer fingerprint reader, a gesture sensor: spoofable, no liveness, no secure element — theatrical, NOT access control); `measurement` (a sensor reading, accurate to its calibration, not a legal/safety instrument); `control` (an output driving a real load — a relay, a motor, a gauge — which gets FAIL-SAFE defaults: known-state on boot/link-loss, e.g. `relay: off`, `gauge: home`). The class is advisory metadata that shapes defaults and documents intent; a match/reading/command carries only the trust its class asserts.
properties.worked: the R503 is `experiential` — the BSG "Permission to Fire" is a CEREMONY (its drama is the point precisely because it isn't real auth); a relay on `[PCB-...]` driving mains is `control` (fail-safe off); an INA219 is `measurement`.

CXC-HALD-MCU.title: The MCU as a Bus Peer — the PCB Port Model (Anchored to Real Boards)

properties.definition: the MCU runs ComposeIO firmware and is a co-equal bus peer: it reads its `on:` peripherals, OWNS each driver (or interprets a descriptor / runs the bytecode VM per its tier), and publishes/subscribes/commands semantic namespaces across the internal-bus↔ComposeBus membrane ([CXC-HALD-BRIDGE]). The PCB exposes I2C buses (Grove-I2C ≡ STEMMA-QT ≡ Qwiic, electrically identical — the density socket, especially with a mux/expander) plus point-to-point analog/digital/PWM/UART ports. The four real boards anchor the model: `[PCB-BTNMATRIX]` (CH32V003, relayed over UART), `[PCB-CANGW]` (CH32V003 + CAN), `[PCB-LEGODOTS]` + `[PCB-GAUGE3]` (ESP32-C3 native WiFi peers) — none is a dumb daughtercard; each has a real brain, so the native-peer `on:` model fits at the top level and the gaps are all one level down (addressing, transport, grouping).

CXC-HALD-BUILT.title: How the Already-Built Drivers Slot In (the Surfacing Answer)

properties.definition: the three drivers built this session are the first realizations, and this schema surfaces them code-free:

the peripheral analog of the widget catalog ([CXC-FEAT-PALETTE], `composer/catalog.py`): a driver-keyed catalog (name, interface kind, `provides?`, default namespaces, addr, config schema, assurance) so a human/Intelligence adds a peripheral in the Composer by picking a driver and assigning a port + namespace — the driver self-description ([CXC-HALD-DRIVER]) generates it. Render widgets → catalog done (this session); peripherals → catalog next.

a running HA instance exposes its state + services over MQTT (its `statestream`) and a WebSocket API. The bridge is a ComposeBus peer that MIRRORS that surface onto the bus, bidirectionally, so any bus participant — a widget, a leaf rule, an Intelligence, another device — reads and commands HA entities as ordinary semantic namespaces, ignorant that HA is behind them. HA runs its own integrations; ComposeIO runs none.

the bridge subscribes HA's state stream (MQTT `statestream` topics `homeassistant/<domain>/<entity>/state`, or the WebSocket `state_changed` events) and publishes each MAPPED entity to a ComposeBus semantic namespace by PHYSICAL QUANTITY ([CXC-HALD-NAMESPACE]) — `sensor.living_room_temp` → `env/temperature`, `binary_sensor.front_door` → `contact/door`, `light.desk` → `light/on` + `light/brightness`. The HA domain + attributes inform the mapping; the bus sees the QUANTITY, not the HA entity id.

a write to a mapped COMMAND namespace becomes an HA SERVICE CALL — `light/on = true` → `light.turn_on{entity_id}`; `light/brightness = 0.5` → `light.turn_on{brightness_pct:50}`; `scene/mood = "storm"` → `scene.turn_on`; `cover/position = 0.3` → `cover.set_cover_position`. Delivered via HA's MQTT command topics or the WebSocket `call_service`. So a ComposeBus director/rule/Intelligence actuates HA-managed devices without knowing HA is behind them — the same `light/on` a native WLED adaptor or an MCU relay consumes.

CXC-HAB-MAPPING.title: The Declarative, Default-Deny Entity ↔ Namespace Map

properties.definition: a declarative map — `{ ha_entity ↔ namespace(s), direction, transform? }` — that is **default-DENY** (only listed entities cross the bridge; a whole HA install does not flood the bus). It reuses the by-physical-quantity vocabulary, so a screen gauge or a leaf rule binds `env/temperature` indifferent to whether a NATIVE sensor or an HA entity is behind it — the define-once payoff, extended across the HA boundary. Auto-SUGGEST from HA's entity registry (domain → default namespace) with explicit overrides; a `transform` handles unit/scale/enum coercion.

the bridge is an `adaptor`-family peer ([CXC-HALD-KINDS] / [CXC-HALD-BUILT]) — a host ComposeApp, sibling to the built WLED adaptor and the Intelligence MCP — configured `interface: { adaptor: { ha: { url, token | mqtt } } }`. Its internal↔ComposeBus membrane ([CXC-HALD-BRIDGE]) EXPORTS the mapped HA namespaces up; IMPORT drives HA. If HA is unreachable it degrades gracefully: the bridged namespaces go `health=down`, and the rest of the bus is UNAFFECTED (encapsulation).

EGRESS (ComposeBus → HA service call) that actuates a real load is AUTHORITY-GATED ([CXC-HALD-BRIDGE] authority), so a random bus peer cannot command HA-managed devices; INGRESS is scoped by the default-deny map (not every HA entity is exported). This is bus hygiene per the HAL membrane model — the same discipline as `gm/cmd/*` and a `control`-class actuator.

CXC-ICV-INTENT.title: The Visual-Fidelity Pass — Refine draw(), Never Break the Wiring

properties.definition: this pass takes the functional MVP and makes it match the pre-vis. CXC-ICV-THEME.title: Theming — a Token Swap, Not a CSS Cascade

properties.definition: the pre-vis themes via CSS custom-property overrides (`:root[data-theme]` + `@media prefers-color-scheme`); the console has no cascade — theme is a TOKEN SWAP. The design-system module ([CXC-ICV-TOKENS]) exposes TWO token tables (`DARK`, `LIGHT`) and a single `active` selector; the scene's `design.theme: dark|light` (already parsed, `parser.py` line 82/373/685) picks the table at mount, and every widget reads `CONSOLE.active.<token>`. Switching theme = re-point `active` + `request_redraw()` — no widget code changes, no per-widget theme branches. DARK is primary (the identity); LIGHT is the legible daylight variant, fully specified in [CXC-ICV-TOKENS]. The header theme button ([CXC-ICV-CHROME]) toggles `active` and redraws.
properties.invariant: NO widget hardcodes a hex or a theme test. A widget that needs a color asks the token by ROLE (`accent`, `crit_dim`, `panel_2`); the role resolves per active table. This is what makes both themes correct from ONE implementation and keeps the two palettes in sync with a single edit.

CXC-ROADMAP.title: ComposeUX Render Engine & Composer — Build Roadmap

properties.definition: ComposeUX is the three-layer render engine of [CXC-R-ARCH] — declarative `.compose.yaml` widgets over a platform-independent engine (layout, hit-test, focus, text, animation, assets) over thin per-platform drawing backends. A widget is authored once and renders pixel-identically on desktop, browser, and CYD. Composer is rebuilt on this engine (ultimately a browser app), previews *real* engine-rendered widgets, and stays bus-native and Intelligence-drivable.
properties.key-insight: CTk is not the foundation — it is the interim runtime the engine is designed to replace ([CXC-R-PHASES]: "Phase 1 replaces CTk widget rendering"). The destination is toolkit-agnostic; CTk retires to the Python/Skia dev-reference role.
properties.status: planned

CXC-RM-RUNTIME-DIST.title: Widget Runtime Distribution (where deployed widgets run)

properties.clarification: This is **runtime-location frequency** — where deployed ComposeUX widgets actually execute in production — NOT development order. By frequency: (1) **macOS**, (2) **Raspberry Pi**, (3) **Browser**. CYD is a low-volume POC tier; mobile is out of scope. (This ranks where *widgets* run; where the *Composer tool* runs is a separate question — see [CXC-RM-M4].)
properties.key-insight: The two highest-frequency runtimes collapse into ONE backend — macOS and RPi both run **Python + Skia** (RPi is a capable Linux/ARM SBC, not a constrained MCU like the CYD). So the workhorse backend, carrying the bulk of production widget execution, is Python-Skia; the browser is the lowest-frequency of the three.
properties.consequence-invest: Backend hardening/perf effort follows frequency — Python-Skia (macOS+RPi) is the workhorse and earns the most investment; the browser backend serves fewer sessions, which relaxes its perf bar and argues against letting it drive the architecture.
properties.consequence-decision1: Because the high-frequency runtimes are Python and mobile is out of scope, keep the engine Python and do NOT adopt Flutter (it would demote the workhorse to reference-only to serve the least-frequent target). Decision 1 narrows to Python-in-browser vs a browser-only re-port — see [CXC-RM-D1].
properties.consequence-dev-order: Development order is set by the critical path ([CXC-RM-PATH]), not by this frequency — but they align: the M0–M2 Python trunk happens to build the two highest-frequency runtimes first; the browser (lowest frequency) is M3.
properties.implication-rpi: Linux/aarch64; fullscreen/kiosk (DRM-KMS or Wayland/X11), possibly rotated. May need skia-python built for aarch64 or a GL surface — a bounded M0 risk. RPi can run the config-driven fungible-display boot ([CXC-R-BOOT]) as a Python app — the middle tier between macOS and CYD.
properties.status: planned

CXC-RM-STATE.title: Two Parallel Worlds; the Hard Bet Is Already Proven

properties.key-insight: The architectural risk is retired. The same widget code renders pixel-comparable on **desktop Skia** and a **resource-starved ESP32/CYD** (ILI9341, 7.6 KB band buffer), verified by a working pixel-diff QA harness. "One tiny contract, render anywhere" is demonstrated, not aspirational.
properties.production-world: `ux_composer/src/composeio_renderers/` — ~11 widgets, each a `CTkFrame` subclass, wired into the dashboard + preview. **Load-bearing. CTk-coupled by design.**
properties.engine-world: `python/composeio/render/` — the `Canvas` contract (ABC) + a real Skia raster backend + `cyd/` C++ backend + 5 agnostic widgets (gauge/led/label/rect/circle). **Not wired into any app.**
gaps-that-define-the-work: Skia backend is raster-only — `present()` is a no-op; **no live window / event loop**.
**No Layer 2 engine** (layout, hit-test, focus, text, gesture, animation) in the agnostic world.
**No `.compose.yaml` runtime** — widgets are constructed programmatically/statically, not parsed from config.
Only 5 of ~16 widgets exist on the contract; the 11 production widgets are CTk-only.
**No browser backend** — the web target is spec + an SSE bus-bridge (`web.py`), zero renderer.
CYD backend implements a *subset* of the contract (no fill_arc/paths/transforms/draw_image/opacity) and has no config-fetch boot.
properties.status: operational (as described)

properties.p1-independently-useful: Every milestone ends in a demonstrable, pixel-verifiable artifact. No milestone is a prerequisite-only stub.
properties.p2-front-load-the-common-trunk: Build what is needed under *every* option first (the Python engine foundation) before resolving the web toolchain fork. This retires CTk on desktop early and de-risks everything downstream.
properties.p3-ctk-stays-until-parity: CTk remains load-bearing until desktop-Skia renders the full production composition from config in a live window. No removal before that gate.
properties.p4-model-stays-agnostic: Nothing new is authored against CTk. Widget definitions are `.compose.yaml` + the `Canvas` contract. The Composer UX redesign (specs/ux/) is toolkit-neutral by construction.
properties.p5-pixel-verified-always: Every backend and widget is regression-tested against the Skia reference via the existing `pixel_comparison.py` harness. Fidelity is a gate, not an afterthought ([CXC-R-C1], [CXC-R-C2]).
properties.p6-bus-native-intelligence-drivable: The engine, its interaction model, and Composer-on-the-engine all remain bus-native; an Intelligence drives and observes identically to a human, over MQTT/websocket.

CXC-RM-D1.title: Decision 1 — In What Language Does Shared Engine+Widget Code Run in the Browser?

properties.decision: OPEN. Must be resolved before [CXC-RM-M3] (browser backend), not before the M0–M2 trunk.
properties.problem-statement: Layer 2 engine + widgets are Python today; CYD is C++ (unavoidable for embedded); a browser cannot run Python natively. So: does the shared code run in-browser as WASM, or is it re-authored in a browser-native language?
properties.context: The two highest-frequency widget runtimes (macOS + RPi) are Python+Skia, mobile is out of scope, and the browser is the *lowest*-frequency of the three ([CXC-RM-RUNTIME-DIST]). So this fork serves one lower-traffic, non-Python target — it must not reshape the whole engine.
properties.option-a: **Pyodide + CanvasKit (WASM).** The one Python engine+widgets run in-browser via Pyodide, drawing through CanvasKit (WASM Skia). Truest define-once — all runtimes run the *same Python code*; C++ only for CYD. Risk: Pyodide payload (multi-MB) + interactive latency — but the browser's low runtime frequency relaxes this bar. Preserves the entire Python investment.
properties.option-b: **Browser-only TypeScript re-port.** Re-author Layer 2 + widgets in TS for the browser alone; a second engine codebase (Python + TS), pixel-verified against the Skia reference. Proven browser perf; bounded because it targets exactly one, lower-frequency platform.
properties.option-c-rejected: **Flutter / Dart.** REJECTED under the current runtime distribution — mobile is out of scope and the browser is lowest-frequency, so Flutter's one-codebase-many-platforms advantage is moot while it would demote the macOS+RPi Python workhorse to reference-only. Revisit only if mobile becomes a significant runtime.
properties.recommendation: Lean **Option A** for define-once; gate on a **time-boxed Pyodide spike** (cold-start payload + interaction latency on a non-trivial `.compose.yaml`). If it fails, fall back to **Option B (browser-only TS)** — one extra codebase for one lower-frequency platform. Not Flutter.
properties.invalidating_assumption: "That mobile stays out of scope and the browser stays low-frequency. If either changes, reopen Flutter. If the Pyodide spike fails, Option B is the fallback."
properties.status: planned

properties.change: "Windowed presentation = SDL2 streaming-texture blit of the SAME raster surface the pixel harness diffs; not a Skia GPU surface."
context_for_change: prior_state: "present() was a no-op; the assumed windowing path was GLFW + Skia GL surface."

reasoning: "Blitting the raster reference makes the on-screen pixels byte-identical to the golden PNGs (verified 100.00% identical), collapsing 'window fidelity' into the existing pixel gate. SDL2 also carries the RPi path (KMSDRM/Wayland/X11) with zero code change, where GLFW cannot do KMSDRM."
rejected_alternative: "GLFW + GPU surface — macOS-deprecated GL, and a GPU rasterizer's AA differs subtly from the raster reference, splitting the golden set."
counter_argument: "CPU raster + full-surface blit may not scale to large/high-DPI surfaces."

counter_response: "Measured: 960x620 full redraw ~1ms, blit <1ms (GL render driver on macOS; Metal driver blocked ~8ms/present and was bypassed). A GPU surface can be added behind SkiaWindow later without touching the Canvas contract."
invalidating_assumption: "That target surfaces stay ≤~2MP at 60fps on CPU raster. If a 4K/120Hz surface becomes a real target, revisit the GPU-surface path."
